newsitem.title: FRANCE: Saint Laurent wins acclaim with return to basics.
newsitem.headline: Saint Laurent wins acclaim with return to basics.

text.p: "Stunning," enthused New York socialite Nan Kempner.
Yves Saint Laurent went back to basics on Wednesday, winning plaudits for the cool elegance of the timeless classics in his spring-summer haute couture show.

You'll never see Saint Laurent's ladies sweat in the easy cut of a classy Prince of Wales trousers suit or the masculine tailoring of a navy serge jacket over a transparent chiffon blouse whose effect ends up ultra-feminine.

From the black tuxedo evening suits that have become wardrobe staples since first introduced three decades ago to the roses nestled in the sloping back of a white evening column, the show was vintage Saint Laurent.
The voices of Judy Garland, Rock Hudson and Doris Day were the backdrop for the Paris presentation.
Supermodel Claudia Schiffer marched out in a sleeveless white number dripping with crystal icicles reminiscent of Marilyn Monroe in the film "Some Like it Hot".
Photographers went wild at the sight as Monroe sang "I'm Through with Love" in the background.
Italian model Carla Bruni slithered down the runway with a bow on the shoulder of her single-strapped navy blue satin gown as poppies bloomed from the bodice of a foamy red tulle.
"He doesn't have to come out with something wild. He just does his thing more beautifully every season," said Kempner, implicitly referring to some of the gimmicks on this season's catwalks.
Deneuve, a close friend of the designer, beamed from behind her sunglasses. "He's someone who never disappoints me. Elegance, refinement, always with such a fantastic sense of colour," she said.
It was the last day of a couture season marked by the dizzying rise of British designers: John Galliano's stunning debut for Dior and Alexander McQueen's anticlimactic first show for Givenchy.
Ready-to-wear designer Thierry Mugler was to top off the five days of collections with his first stab at haute couture later in the day.

Late on Tuesday, Christian Lacroix dreamed up wildly luxurious mixes of textiles and textures with a Far Eastern flavour for the 10th anniversary of his fashion house, winning the loudest applause of the season.

Organza, satin, taffeta, tulle and lace -- each dress was a sumptuous collage of fabrics and genres as Lacroix embarked on a lone, mad voyage into a universe of imaginary women. The clothes were more the work of an immensely imaginative artist than a dressmaker -- beautiful to look at but hard to wear.
Like a magician, he crafted saffron, pomegranate, flame and tea-rose silks into ornately draped gowns, many embroidered with gold and jewels worthy of a maharanee.

"Women are always looking for individuality and freedom," Lacroix told a crowd of admirers after the show. "It's not because there's a dictatorship that says everything should be black or Zen that it should be obeyed. Women want to be themselves and our duty is to give them that."
